描述_ZN: The Fisherman's Father" scroll, Yuan, by Wu Zhen, on silk, ink and brush, 84.7 cm long, 29.7 cm wide.　　In ancient China, fishing, woodcutting, farming, and reading were often considered idealized lifestyles by literati and scholars, and were often used as themes for literary works to express the author's desire to escape from the world, with the material of "fishing and seclusion" being the most common. During the Yuan Dynasty, Han literati had no way to enter society and their social status plummeted, and this was especially true for the Jiangnan scholars. As a result, "fishermen and hermits" appeared more frequently in paintings, among which Wu Zhen's "Fishermen and Fathers" is the most typical. Wu Zhen was good at landscape painting with the theme of "fishermen and hermits", and there are several copies of "Fisherman's Father", of which this is one of the more representative ones. The picture depicts the scenery of the south of the Yangtze River, with trees on a flat hill and a fisherman's father driving a boat to escape between the bend of the lake and the color of the water. The ink is pale and moist, and the rocks, trees, branches and leaves are all used in alternating shades of ink to show the hierarchical relationship and highlight the main objects. The varied brushwork, chafing and dabbing, all show the author's superb brush control. The secluded and quiet mood of the lake and mountains leaps off the paper, giving a sense of being far away from the mundane. Wu Zhen's "Fisherman's Father" is mostly matched by the powerful and dashing cursive script "Fisherman's Father Group", which complements poetry, calligraphy and painting. The poem, calligraphy, and painting complement each other well. For example, in this picture, it reads: "The frost and fading maple leaves are blurred. A thousand feet of waves, four gills of perch, and a gourd of wine in a poetry tube." The poem punctuates the picture, and truly expresses the hermitage of "one leaf follows the wind for ten thousand miles".
